companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
PepsiCo, the second-largest food and beverage company in the world, grappled with inflation in 2022. The rising cost of goods forced the brand behind products like Doritos, Lay’s, Gatorade, and Pepsi to hike prices on some of its own products, which boosted revenue but hurt demand as consumers cut discretionary spending.

  • PepsiCo's net revenue for the fiscal year grew 8.7% to $86.4 billion, and the operating profit on its North America beverage segment rose 122% to $5.43 billion year over year following its sale of some juice brands in 2021.

  • PepsiCo expects organic revenue growth to be slower in 2023, and plans to buy back roughly $1 billion worth of shares to shore up its finances.

  • PepsiCo plans to roll out Tesla electric delivery trucks in 2023.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: PepsiCo is the second-largest food and beverage company in the world, known for household snacks such as Cheetos and Doritos, as well as beverages like Gatorade, Pepsi, and Mountain Dew. The company’s revenue rose 13% in 2021 as consumer spending rebounded broadly from the worst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But PepsiCo has forecast that inflation in prices for ingredients and higher shipping costs will hurt its prospects in 2022. The continuing Ukraine-Russia conflict has also negatively affected the beverage giant. In April 2022 the company reported more than $400 million in impairment charges related to its loss of business in the two nations.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: PepsiCo saw a boost in sales of snacks and breakfast foods like oatmeal and pancakes as more consumers ate at home more often during the pandemic—a shift that helped push revenue over the $70 billion mark, a nearly 5% increase over the prior year. But soda sales were soft as venues like restaurants and arenas closed, and profits declined 2.7%, with the beverage and snacking giant spending some $800 million on COVID-19–related costs. The company has made big investments in e-commerce, launching two direct-to-consumer websites and acquiring Chinese online snack company Be & Cheery. CEO Ramon Laguarta, now in his third year on the job, has continued PepsiCo’s sustainability push, including the company’s recent commitments to regenerative agriculture.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: PepsiCo continued its quest to offer consumers healthier food and beverage options in 2019, with the acquisitions of Hormel's CytoSport business, which makes Muscle Milk protein shakes, and BFY Brands, producer of PopCorner snacks. Ramon Laguarta, the successor to longtime CEO Indra Nooyi, ended his first year on the job with strong revenues of $67.1 billion, up from $64.7 billion in 2018. Now he finds himself with a pandemic to navigate. While quarantining consumers stocked up on Quaker products and Tostitos chips, an expected lag in beverage sales at gas stations and restaurants compelled PepsiCo, an advertising stalwart, to curtail its marketing spend in early 2020.

companyRankingLists.description: Global business is back. After limping through a worldwide financial crisis and economic slowdown, the 500 largest companies ranked by revenues shattered all sorts of performance records in 2013: They racked up combined revenues of $31.1 trillion, up 2.5% from 2012, and profits soared 27% to nearly $2 trillion. China’s 95 companies (up from 89 last year) posted $5.8 trillion in revenues. The U.S. has four fewer companies on the list than last year but remains (for now) the country leader, with 128 corporations on the list—including No. 1 Wal-Mart Stores—reporting $8.6 trillion in revenues.
